10.1111/1475-679x.12053.title: The Impact of Recognition Versus Disclosure on Financial Information: A Preparer's Perspective
10.1111/1475-679x.12053.research_question: Does recognition versus footnote disclosure affect managers' contingent-liability estimates?
10.1111/1475-679x.12053.sample: Experiment with corporate controllers and CFOs at public and private companies; sample size and collection period not stated in abstract.
10.1111/1475-679x.12053.identification: Experiment varying recognition versus disclosure placement and comparing public- and private-company managers.
10.1111/1475-679x.12053.main_findings: Public-company managers expend more cognitive effort, exhibit less strategic bias, and report higher liability estimates under recognition than disclosure. The analogous placement effects are absent among private-company managers.

10.1016/j.jacceco.2014.08.007.title: Mandatory disclosure and asymmetry in financial reporting
10.1016/j.jacceco.2014.08.007.research_question: Why might managers collectively favor disclosure rules requiring more disclosure about adverse events?
10.1016/j.jacceco.2014.08.007.identification: Model of political influence in which a majority of informed managers chooses mandatory disclosure rules.
10.1016/j.jacceco.2014.08.007.main_findings: Equilibrium rules require greater disclosure of adverse events. Asymmetry increases with measurement informativeness, verifiability, and ex ante uncertainty.

10.2308/tar-2018-0262.title: Voluntary Disclosure Responses to Mandated Disclosure: Evidence from Australian Corporate Tax Transparency
10.2308/tar-2018-0262.research_question: How do firms supplement mandated public tax-return disclosures?
10.2308/tar-2018-0262.sample: Australian corporate tax-transparency setting; years and sample size not stated in abstract.
10.2308/tar-2018-0262.identification: Empirical analysis of supplemental voluntary disclosure around mandated tax disclosure; exact estimator not stated in abstract.
10.2308/tar-2018-0262.main_findings: Firms anticipating reputational costs from unexpectedly low disclosed tax liabilities issue preemptive and supplemental information, particularly when supplemental disclosure has low proprietary costs.

10.1007/s11142-026-09962-3.title: Tax numbers and ETR forecasting
10.1007/s11142-026-09962-3.research_question: What determines numeric tax disclosure, and how does it relate to analysts' implied ETR forecasts?
10.1007/s11142-026-09962-3.sample: Financial-statement tax disclosures; sample period and size not stated in abstract.
10.1007/s11142-026-09962-3.identification: Empirical analysis of disclosure determinants and forecast outcomes; causal identification not stated in abstract.
10.1007/s11142-026-09962-3.main_findings: More tax numbers are associated with lower implied ETR forecast errors and dispersion, particularly numbers in footnotes. Narrative emphasis does not provide the same reduction in information frictions.

10.1111/1475-679x.12617.title: Tax Strategy Disclosure: A Greenwashing Mandate?
10.1111/1475-679x.12617.research_question: Does mandated qualitative tax-strategy disclosure improve transparency and tax compliance?
10.1111/1475-679x.12617.sample: Large businesses affected by the 2016 UK tax-strategy disclosure reform; observation period and sample size not stated in abstract.
10.1111/1475-679x.12617.identification: Uses the 2016 UK reform as an exogenous disclosure shock; precise estimator not stated in abstract.
10.1111/1475-679x.12617.main_findings: Affected firms increase tax-strategy disclosure, but it becomes more boilerplate. The study finds no significant tax-planning response despite increased media attention.

10.1111/1475-679x.12151.title: Do PCAOB Inspections Improve the Quality of Internal Control Audits?
10.1111/1475-679x.12151.source: OpenAlex via search_journals; publisher abstract verified. Publisher assigns volume 55 to 2017; first online publication was September 12, 2016.
10.1111/1475-679x.12151.research_question: Do PCAOB inspection findings improve internal-control audit quality?
10.1111/1475-679x.12151.sample: U.S. internal-control audit and inspection setting; sample years and size not stated in abstract.
10.1111/1475-679x.12151.identification: Cross-sectional and time-series inspection-content variation with audit-firm and year fixed effects, described by the authors as effectively a difference-in-differences design.
10.1111/1475-679x.12151.main_findings: Higher reported deficiency rates predict more adverse internal-control opinions, including for clients with concurrent misstatements, and higher audit fees. ([onlinelibrary.wiley.com](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1475-679X.12151?utm_source=openai))

10.2308/ajpt-50752.title: PCAOB Quality Control Inspection Reports and Auditor Reputation
10.2308/ajpt-50752.venue: Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory
10.2308/ajpt-50752.research_question: Does public disclosure of unremediated quality-control criticism affect auditor reputation?
10.2308/ajpt-50752.sample: PCAOB-inspected audit firms; sample period and size not stated in abstract.
10.2308/ajpt-50752.identification: Examines audit-firm market-share changes following public disclosure of Part II quality-control criticism.
10.2308/ajpt-50752.main_findings: Audit firms lose significant market share following public disclosure of quality-control criticisms.

10.1093/rfs/hhad002.title: Climate Risk Disclosure and Institutional Investors
10.1093/rfs/hhad002.research_question: Do institutional investors demand and influence corporate climate-risk disclosure?
10.1093/rfs/hhad002.sample: Institutional-investor survey and observational holdings data; sample period and size not stated in abstract.
10.1093/rfs/hhad002.identification: Survey, holdings analyses, and a shock to French institutional investors' disclosure demand under Article 173.
10.1093/rfs/hhad002.main_findings: Investors report strong demand for climate disclosure and engagement. Climate-conscious ownership is positively associated with better disclosure, with additional evidence from the French demand shock.

10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.title: The impact of carbon disclosure mandates on emissions and financial operating performance
10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.source: OpenAlex via search_journals; publisher full text verified
10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.research_question: Does mandatory carbon reporting change emissions and operating performance?
10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.sample: UK-incorporated listed firms affected by the 2013 mandate versus other European listed firms; ten-year window around 2013. Exact sample size not extracted.
datasets: Ownership Links and Enhanced EUTL Dataset Project
10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.identification: Difference-in-differences linking installation-level verified emissions to ultimate owners.
10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x.main_findings: Affected firms reduce emissions by about 8% relative to controls without a significant gross-margin change. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11142-021-09611-x))

10.2308/tar-2017-0550.title: Complementarity between Audited Financial Reporting and Voluntary Disclosure: The Case of Former Andersen Clients
10.2308/tar-2017-0550.research_question: Are audited reporting quality and voluntary disclosure complementary?
10.2308/tar-2017-0550.sample: Former Arthur Andersen clients forced to change auditors; exact years and sample size not stated in abstract.
10.2308/tar-2017-0550.identification: Uses forced auditor changes and cross-sectional changes in financial-reporting quality.
10.2308/tar-2017-0550.main_findings: Former Andersen clients increase forecast frequency, precision, and specificity after changing auditors; larger reporting-quality improvements accompany larger disclosure increases.
theories: Complementarity between audited and voluntary reporting

10.2308/accr-51936.title: Banks' Financial Reporting Frequency and Asset Quality
10.2308/accr-51936.research_question: Does quarterly reporting affect banks' loan quality and risk-taking?
10.2308/accr-51936.sample: Banks observed from 2000 to 2014; sample size not stated in abstract.
10.2308/accr-51936.identification: Examines banks switching to quarterly disclosure; precise estimator not stated in abstract.
10.2308/accr-51936.main_findings: Switching banks experience an approximately 11% relative decline in nonperforming loans and lower deposit rates and CDS spreads, consistent with market discipline.

10.2139/ssrn.5542138.title: Anticipating Change: Stock Market and Firm Responses to Disaggregation in Income Tax Disclosures
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.venue: SSRN; also presented at 2026 FARS and EAA meetings
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.source: search_ssrn; SSRN abstract recovered by web search; 2026 FARS program verified
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.research_question: How do investors and managers anticipate ASU 2023-09?
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.sample: Firms with differing exposure to ASU 2023-09; years and sample size not stated in abstract. SSRN revision dated February 4, 2026.
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.identification: Relative stock returns around standard-setting milestones and exposure-related reporting responses.
10.2139/ssrn.5542138.main_findings: More exposed firms have positive relative milestone returns and reduce disclosed tax risk. The authors attribute the short-run risk reduction to reporting discretion rather than reduced tax avoidance. ([papers.ssrn.com](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5542138&utm_source=openai))

10.2139/ssrn.7355339.title: The Value of Tax Transparency
10.2139/ssrn.7355339.source: search_ssrn; SSRN abstract recovered by web search
10.2139/ssrn.7355339.research_question: How do investors respond to first-time jurisdiction-level tax disclosures under ASU 2023-09?
10.2139/ssrn.7355339.sample: First ASU 2023-09-compliant Forms 10-K; sample size not stated in abstract. Revised September 18, 2026.
datasets: SEC EDGAR Form 10-K and Exhibit 21 disclosures
10.2139/ssrn.7355339.identification: Filing-window return associations with disclosed rate-lowering jurisdictions, haven versus non-haven comparisons, and prior-year filing comparisons.
10.2139/ssrn.7355339.main_findings: Positive filing-window return associations concentrate in disclosures identifying rate-lowering tax havens; the authors report no comparable positive prior-year association. This is not presented here as randomized causal evidence. ([papers.ssrn.com](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7355339&utm_source=openai))

10.2139/ssrn.7220660.title: Staying under the radar: The case of sustainability disclosures in the US
10.2139/ssrn.7220660.venue: SSRN; TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper No. 244
10.2139/ssrn.7220660.research_question: Do U.S. firms camouflage sustainability reporting or substantively retrench amid the anti-ESG turn?
10.2139/ssrn.7220660.sample: 10-K reports from 2020–2025 and firms' SASB adoption data; sample size not stated in abstract.
datasets: SASB adoption data; provider not stated in abstract
10.2139/ssrn.7220660.identification: Disclosure-pattern analysis with U.S. versus non-U.S. comparisons for SASB adoption; a clean causal design is not stated in abstract.
10.2139/ssrn.7220660.main_findings: Salient ESG terminology and framework affiliation decline first; broader topic coverage changes less sharply. By 2025, sustainability-text length and action mentions also weaken. The authors cannot fully distinguish camouflage from broader retrenchment. ([accounting-for-transparency.de](https://www.accounting-for-transparency.de/de/publications/no-244-staying-under-the-radar-the-case-of-sustainability-disclosures-in-the-us/?utm_source=openai))
